lesson.title: Seeing Voltage Through Time: How an Oscilloscope Works
lesson.summary: An oscilloscope draws a picture of an electrical signal by plotting voltage on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis, turning something you cannot see into a shape you can read and measure.
lesson.body:
You already know that voltage is the electrical potential difference that pushes current through a circuit, and that a sinusoidal waveform repeats itself over and over with a fixed period, the time it takes to complete one cycle. The trouble is that voltage itself is invisible. A multimeter can tell you a single number, like "3.3 volts," but it cannot show you how that voltage is changing from one instant to the next. An oscilloscope solves this problem by drawing a graph in real time: the vertical axis represents voltage, the horizontal axis represents time, and the resulting trace is literally a picture of the signal's shape.

The screen of an oscilloscope is divided into a grid of squares, and two settings control what each square means. The vertical setting, called volts per division (volts/div), tells you how many volts each square represents; the horizontal setting, called time per division (time/div or sec/div), tells you how much time each square represents. If you set the vertical control to 1 volt/div and a waveform's peak reaches two squares above the center line, that waveform's peak is 2 volts. The same logic applies horizontally: you read off how many divisions a repeating feature of the waveform spans, then multiply by the time/div setting to find how much real time that feature took.

This is exactly how you measure a period on a scope. Suppose the time/div control is set to 2 milliseconds per division, and one complete cycle of a sine wave, say, from one peak to the next identical peak, spans exactly 5 horizontal divisions. The period is then T = 5 divisions times 2 ms/div = 10 ms. Once you have the period, you already know from your work with periodic waveforms that frequency is simply its reciprocal, so this signal repeats at f = 1/T = 1/0.010 s = 100 Hz. The oscilloscope did not tell you the frequency directly; it gave you a picture from which you could read the period, and from the period you calculated the frequency yourself.

For this picture to be readable at all, the trace has to hold still: each new sweep across the screen needs to start at the same point in the waveform's cycle as the last one, or the image would smear into a scrolling blur. The circuit that makes that happen is called triggering, and it deserves its own detailed treatment later; for now, just know that a properly triggered scope is what makes a stable, measurable trace possible in the first place. Most oscilloscopes also offer two or more input channels, so you can display two signals on the same time axis at once, a capability you will rely on later when comparing the timing relationship between two waveforms.
